title: Features: report rendering
summary:
This part settles what authors and readers get when RichView renders a report: the document shell, header and link-preview tags, Markdown prose, every block except charts (table, metric, callout, image, audio, video, embed), how failures show in drafts, styles and the `theme` option as authors meet them, motion and the readiness hook, the self-contained file and `Rendered/` folder, data and media embedding, supported browsers, browser print, PDF and other outputs, accessibility and language. Charts are part 04a, CLI, server, MCP and editor surfaces 04c, branch-only features 04d, field types 05 and style tokens 06; items here point to them instead of repeating them. Behaviour was read at `b4db233` (2026-10-16) and checked with the release build and headless Chromium on 2026-10-21 and 2026-10-22; new captures are in `docs/lockdown/screenshots/report-rendering/`. Fixture figures come from `docs/lockdown/screenshots/product/fixture/source/` rendered with its four media files (image, tone, clip and poster), which are not kept beside it; without them `generate` stops with four `report.asset.missing` errors.

The decisions that change the most:

- **`theme` (FEA-RP-33)**: the light/dark override goes. Today it breaks chart contrast while `check` reports clean, and on a server that also hosts the showcase it silently restyles the report. ARC-06, INT-56 and TYP-69 still assume it.
- **Failures in drafts (FEA-RP-29 to FEA-RP-31, FEA-RP-57, FEA-RP-58)**: a broken block, missing file or broken link fails only its element with a notice in place, misspelled tags and unreadable frontmatter are flagged, and the in-report report card goes, which part 04c already follows. Today one missing image or linked file aborts the whole render.
- **PDF (FEA-RP-43, FEA-RP-44)**: PDF export stays, enters `dev` only with its pagination fixtures passing, and refuses reports with errors. Today’s fixture PDF splits its metrics across two pages and ends with a page holding only the colophon.
- **Leaner Markdown (FEA-RP-05, FEA-RP-12 to FEA-RP-14, FEA-RP-53)**: prolog, wikilinks, pull quotes and raw HTML leave, HTML comments, which today ship in the published file, are dropped, and rich blocks sit only at the top level.
- **Weight (FEA-RP-38)**: the 2.1 MB runtime is embedded only when a report has a chart or table block; a one-paragraph report weighs 2.37 MB today.
- **Against Daniel’s own requests**: FEA-RP-35 keeps report text still, reversing his 2026-06-27 request for “beautiful soft animations of chart and texts”.
- **S27-616’s outputs (FEA-RP-42, FEA-RP-46 to FEA-RP-48)**: following Daniel’s INT-31 answer, hosted media arrive through pinned asset references, scrollytelling is built as an element inside a report, and the carousel PDF and per-output markers are dropped.
- **Accessibility and privacy (FEA-RP-49, FEA-RP-55, FEA-RP-56)**: WCAG 2.2 AA becomes the standard, checked by the dev gate’s accessibility audit (DEL-58), audio and video gain captions and transcripts, and embeds load only when the reader asks.

Answer each card: **accept** keeps the proposal as the rewrite’s rule (where options are listed, the proposal is the recommended option; FEA-RP-24 keeps today’s layout because no evidence settles it), **edit** replaces it with your text, **reject** drops the feature or rule from the rewrite, and **defer** leaves it open. A card that removes or adds a format field names the part 05 item it changes under conflicts; answer both the same way. Part 08's cross-part contradiction cards (OPN-50 to OPN-68) decide conflicts involving this part's cards and should be answered first.

items.title: The source stays canonical; renders are reproducible
items.question: Do renders leave the `.rmd`, its data and style files untouched, and give byte-identical HTML for identical inputs?
items.why: Git-native publishing (INT-22), the visual gate (DEL-28) and review diffs compare outputs. Daniel's INT-13 answer makes trust in the output the target: the same source renders consistently, to a high standard, every time. A renderer that edits sources, or stamps times and paths into the HTML, would break the plain-text contract (INT-04) and make every diff noisy.
items.proposed: Rendering reads the report folder and writes only under `Rendered/`; it never rewrites the `.rmd`, its data or its style files. The same source, inputs, styles and RichView build produce byte-identical HTML and the same PDF pages. Nothing time-, machine- or path-dependent enters the HTML: generated ids are positional, and drawn marks such as pencil strokes stay seeded.

items.title: HTML document shell
items.question: Is this the document every report renders into?
items.why: Today the shell carries a charset, a viewport, the title and `<meta name="generator" content="richview/3.0.0-alpha.0">`, and `lang` is always `en`. This card adds the report language (TYP-08), the Content Security Policy that ARC-15 requires in exported files, a colour-scheme hint, and a generator tag naming the build commit, because the commit identifies every build, while the public meaning of version numbers is open now that Daniel's INT-71 answer lists the extension and offers builds from `prod` (DEL-41). Link-preview tags are FEA-RP-51.
items.proposed: Every report is one HTML5 document: `<html lang>` from `lang` (TYP-08); charset and viewport; `<title>` from the title; the Content Security Policy `<meta>` of ARC-15; `<meta name="color-scheme">` naming the active style’s scheme, `dark` or `light`; and `<meta name="generator">` naming RichView and its build commit. The body is one `<article>` with `<header>`, `<main>` and `<footer>`. All CSS sits in one `<style>`; the only scripts are inert JSON payloads and the report runtime (ARC-13).

items.title: Link-preview and search tags
items.question: Should a report carry a description and Open Graph tags, so a shared link shows its title and deck?
items.why: Today a report carries no `<meta name="description">` and no Open Graph tags, so a link pasted into a chat, an email or a post shows a bare address or the page title, and search results quote arbitrary text. `description` already holds the deck (FEA-RP-04), and TYP-07 would require it to publish.
items.proposed: `<meta name="description">` and `og:description` carry `description`, `og:title` carries the title, and `og:type` is `article`. A report without a description carries neither description tag. A story at an address on a host also carries `og:image`, its alt text and `twitter:card` `summary_large_image`, pointing at the thumbnail its host renders (FEA-SF-55, INT-07). A self-contained file opened from disk has no absolute address and carries no `og:image`. The self-contained file a host offers for download is the embedded-mode render and carries no `og:` tags either. A story shared only with signed-in readers serves no title, description or image to anyone who is not signed in, so a link preview never reveals a private story (INT-07, OPN-54).

items.title: Report header
items.question: Is this the header: optional image, title, deck and byline, with the header image named like any other image?
items.why: Today a path-only `title_image` takes the report title as its alt text, so screen readers hear the title twice; the header image accepts three alias keys; and the date prints exactly as typed.
items.proposed: The header shows, in order: the optional header image, the title as the page’s only `<h1>`, the deck (FEA-RP-04) and a byline with author and date. The header image follows the image block (T-BLOCK-IMAGE): `alt` is required, `""` marks it decorative, and the title is never reused as alt text; a bare path is treated as decorative and warns that `alt` is missing. The date shows in the report language’s long form (FEA-RP-50). Drafts without a title show “Untitled report”. Choosing, cropping and crediting the image: FEA-RP-52.

items.title: Header imagery: choice, crop and credit
items.question: How do authors choose, crop and credit a header image, and what may it claim?
items.why: S27-616 asks for illustrative header imagery “as a normal choice for most reports, with author control over selection, replacement, crop and omission”, and S27-637 for a visible attribution that matches each image’s licence. FEA-RP-03 fixes only the header’s order and alt text, and INT-75 only the flagship’s graphic. Today `title_image` takes the image fields, cropping does not work (`fit` has no visible effect, FEA-RP-26), the credit sits in the caption by convention, and nothing checks that a header graphic’s figures are sourced in the report (the flagship’s header is a chart image whose figures the body repeats with sources).
items.proposed: A header image stays optional and is chosen, replaced or removed through `title_image` alone; `richview learn` presents a credited header image as a normal choice for most reports. It crops like an image block: `width` and `height` set its aspect ratio and `fit: cover` fills that box (FEA-RP-26). Its credit goes in the `credit` field that Daniel's FEA-RP-62 answer gives image blocks and `title_image` (author, author_url, source, source_url), printed under the image in small type, and `caption` describes the image; `richview check` notes (`info`) a header image with neither credit nor caption and warns on an `images.unsplash.com` photo without a credit (FEA-RP-62). `richview image search` and `richview image use` find a photo. Header imagery is one of the tools RichView gives authors (Daniel's INT-77 answer); RichView does not judge whether an image suits the story. A header image may illustrate or summarise, but it states no figure the report does not source; a header graphic that must follow the active style is drawn by the renderer from the report’s data (INT-75), not supplied as an image file.

items.title: Code blocks
items.question: How do ordinary fenced code blocks render: plain, in the style’s mono face, or highlighted?
items.why: Only inline code gets the style’s mono face; `pre code` falls back to the browser’s default monospace, so the fixture PDF reports 137 glyphs drawn in Menlo (`export.font-fallback`). A highlighter for Rich Markdown, YAML and shell exists, but only the site uses it.
items.proposed:
A fenced code block renders as preformatted text in the style's mono face at the small size. On screen it scrolls sideways inside its own box; on paper it wraps, each wrapped line hanging from its own indent. An info string of SQL, Rich Markdown, YAML or shell (such as `sql`, `rmd`, `yaml` or `sh`) is highlighted as below; any other leaves the code plain.

The label, the title, line numbers and marks belong to the `code` block. Its head shows `lang` as the language label and `title`, a file name or caption, and it has three more fields:

- `lines`: line numbers, which are never copied with the code.
- `mark`: lines and ranges such as `5-6`, set as a rule plus a tint, never colour alone. A mark past the last line warns `code.mark`.
- `src`: a UTF-8 text file of the report folder, given instead of `text`. It holds 400 lines at most; a longer file is a `block.schema` error that says to excerpt it.

Code is text and is never executed. Diagram languages such as `mermaid` are code like any other.

Highlight at build time. Keys and keywords take the accent hue, strings a warm hue, and numbers, booleans, null and YAML dates a third hue from the style’s chart series. Use the resolved chart palette for custom colours. Comments and punctuation use soft ink, and unmarked text uses the main ink. On both ordinary and marked lines each role reaches 4.5:1. The three coloured roles have chroma at least 0.09 on light surfaces and 0.07 on dark, with 45 degrees between their hues. Hand-drawn uses its graphite inks and the code face’s weight. Paper keeps the same roles with the paper palette. Use the code face's 600 for structure and its italic for comments only where the style embeds those faces. Every other language is plain.

`code` is a rich fence tag, so a plain fence whose info string is `code` is now read as the block; a listing written that way needs another info string.

items.title: Columns
items.question: Can an author put two to four blocks side by side, such as two charts, a chart beside its explanation or a row of metrics?
items.why: Daniel called blocks and columns a huge priority on 18 November 2026. Every block stacks in one column today, so a chart and the sentence that explains it, or three headline numbers, can only follow one another.
items.proposed:
A `::: columns` line opens two to four columns, each `::: column` holds one column and a line of `:::` closes each column and the columns, the fenced-div shape of Pandoc, Quarto and MyST. A column holds prose, headings of level 3 and below and rich blocks with their source notes, written as at the top level. It cannot hold other columns, a scrolly block, a level 1 or 2 heading or the heading a tab or a collapsed section starts at.

The options after `::: columns` are a YAML flow mapping of closed vocabulary, checked like a block's fields: `widths` (`equal`, or a ratio such as `2-1` or `1-2-1`), `gap` (`small`, `medium`, `large`), `align` (`top`, `center`, `bottom`) and `wide` (default `true`: the report's width; `false` keeps the text measure). No author writes a class, a style or a length.

Reading order is source order. The columns stand side by side while the narrowest would be at least its floor, a phone's column for a chart, table, frame, video or code and 11rem otherwise, and stack, all of them, below it; the same rule holds on paper, where a column is not split and a PDF's float and fit pass treats the whole columns box as one unit, so a chart in a column is never floated or fitted on its own. On a phone they always stack. A chart is laid out at its column's width, and between a phone and the width where the columns stand side by side at the stacked column's width, so the box the page reserves matches the runtime's layout above the width where the columns stand side by side and on a phone, and comes within a few pixels of it between them.

A value outside the vocabulary (`widths: 70%`) is a `block.schema` error, as in a block, and leaves the markers as text.

Columns that are not well formed warn with their own `columns.*` code and every line stays as it was, so the content renders in one column exactly as it would without columns. Other fenced divs stay text without a warning.

Rows beyond `max_rows` sit in a native disclosure labelled “Showing N of M rows” (TYP-24) directly below, continuing the same columns; the total row comes after all rows. items.title: Heat in table cells
items.question: Can an author shade a numeric column of a table by value, so the table reads as a heat map while every number stays printed?
items.why: Daniel asked on 16 November 2026 for tables with heat maps, sorting and filtering. A table cell has no shade today: a `heatmap` chart exists, but a table whose point is one column, or a matrix of numbers, can only print them.
items.proposed:
`columns[n].heat` shades the cells of a numeric column by value. `true` or `sequential` runs from the column's lowest value, which stays unshaded, to its highest; `diverging` shades both sides of zero, which stays unshaded, with the style's negative colour below it and equal distances equally strong. `heat_scale: table` puts the heat columns of one kind on one scale, so the table reads as a matrix; the default, `column`, gives each its own. Heat is off unless the author names a column. No author writes a colour.

The shade is the style's own heat colour, the one its heatmap charts use (`chart.ramp`, and `chart.negative-ramp` for the negative arm), so it follows a brand colour and the scheme. It is mixed into the page only as far as `ink` keeps 7:1 on it (STY-25): the strongest shade is capped, the number is printed in the page's ink and nothing flips. Every cell prints its number, so the shade is never the only carrier and there is no colour key. A style whose two heat colours are one, as Hand-drawn's graphite is, hatches the cells below zero, as its charts do. Paper keeps the shades.

A cell's shade comes from the value the cell shows, at the precision it shows, in whole percent of the column's shown range: cells that show the same number share a shade, and the page holds no finer value (FEA-CH-37). A number its cell cannot show, a percent past what a number holds (`inf%`), has no shade and no sort value, so such cells tie. Sorting keeps a shade with its row. The total row, empty and missing cells and text cells are not shaded. `heat` on a column that is not all numbers warns `table.heat` and the column stays plain; a value outside the vocabulary is a `block.schema` error. A report without a heat column carries none of the rules.

items.title: Filtering a table
items.question: Can a reader filter the rows of a table by typing, without the author writing anything?
items.why: Daniel asked on 16 November 2026 for tables with heat maps, sorting and filtering. A long table can be sorted and folds at `max_rows`, but a reader looking for one region or one name has to read every row.
items.proposed:
A table gets a filter box: one search field above its rows and under its title, labelled “Filter rows” in the page's language. Typing keeps the rows whose shown text holds every typed word in any column, whatever the case or accents; Escape or the field's clear button empties it. `filter` is `auto` by default, which shows the box for a table of more than 10 rows; `true` and `false` decide.

The runtime adds the field, as it does the sort buttons, so the static page has no dead control: without scripts the table is the plain table, and a PDF has no field and every row. Slides (FEA-RP-65) show a table without the box, as they show a chart without the report’s tools. A page that runs scripts keeps the line's room under the title from the first paint, so neither the title nor the rows move when the box arrives; if the runtime has not started after 10 s, when the page's charts say so too, the room is given back. In a narrow table the field shrinks beside its label, so the empty box keeps to the one line its room holds; only the status line, which typing brings, may take a second.

A status line beside the field says what the filter did, politely to a screen reader: “7 of 64 rows”, or “No rows match” while the table keeps its headings and, when it has one, its total. Rows that do not match are hidden, so they leave the accessibility tree; focus never moves while typing. The field is a real search input with a visible label, before the table in the tab order. Matching rows fill the first `max_rows` places and the rest stay under the fold, whose line reads “Showing 20 of 57 matching rows”. Sorting orders the matching rows and the filter keeps the sort (FEA-RP-22). A `total` row stays the total of every row, and while a filter is on the status line says so (FEA-RP-21). The browser's print shows the rows in view and the filter's text.

options.label: Build as proposed
options.detail: A search box added by the runtime, on above 10 rows, with a status line; the total stays the total of every row.

options.label: An authored `controls` filter, as on charts
options.detail: One vocabulary with charts and a defined printed state, but the author has to write it and a reader can only pick the listed values.

options.label: Only when the author asks
options.detail: No change to existing reports, but most long tables would never get one.

items.recommendation: Build as proposed: it needs no author work, and a long table is where a reader looks for one row.

items.title: What moves in a report
items.question: Which parts of a report move: chart data only, or also the blocks of text as they enter?
items.why: On 2026-06-27 Daniel asked for “beautiful soft animations of chart and texts”, and the TypeScript renderer of July faded text and charts up. Commit `4167940` (2026-10-11, merged with PR #22 for S27-616) removed “the load-time text and chart fades”; charts keep their own entrances (FEA-CH-51), and MOTION.md now says report text never animates. The lockdown evidence records no later statement from Daniel asking for still text. The vNext study proposed one text motion, a staggered fade-up. Daniel's INT-12 answer (2026-10-27) now sets the bar for all motion: delightful and smooth, the whimsical quality of Studio Ghibli meeting the polish of Apple's website animations, with motion that explains structure or change and gives pleasure counted as craft.
items.proposed: Report motion serves the bar of Daniel's INT-12 answer: delightful and smooth, in the spirit of Studio Ghibli's whimsy and Apple's website polish. Chart data moves as FEA-CH-51 and FEA-CH-52 specify. Blocks below the first screen (titles, prose, metrics, callouts, tables, media) enter once with one soft fade-up of about 300 ms as they come into view. Blocks that come into view together stagger by at most four steps, so a long run of blocks never waits on its own entrance. The runtime applies it, so the first screen, print, PDF and a report without scripts show every word at rest (FEA-RP-39); an entrance never delays reading and never repeats when the reader scrolls back. Under reduced motion nothing animates (FEA-RP-36). Scrollytelling figures move as FEA-RP-48 says. All of it passes INT-61's phone-smoothness floor and the filmstrip evidence (DEL-30); a style that switches motion off (TYP-49, STY-15) renders everything settled. Any further motion a style adds is part of that style's design review (STY-01), judged by a review agent (INT-12, DEL-68).

items.title: PDF export
items.question: Does RichView keep exporting reports to PDF (`generate --to pdf`), and what must every PDF get right on the page?
items.why: Daniel’s 2026-10-10 product brief asks for a readable report PDF (S27-616), and INT-04 names it the print output. The export works (fixture: 9 A4 pages, about 490 KB, 0.8 to 3.1 s, tagged with an outline) but misses the bar: the colophon sits alone on page 9, the metrics split across pages 6 and 7, keep-together rules leave pages half empty, and code prints in a system font. PR #22 left eleven pagination findings open, and `verify-exports.mjs` did not run in the lockdown checks. ARC-30 leaves both the keep decision and this bar to this card.
items.proposed: Keep. `richview generate <report> --to pdf` prints through a local Chromium-family browser (ARC-30) to A4 or Letter: charts settled, network blocked, light paper, running title and page numbers from page 2, tags and an outline. Charts reach the PDF as vector output (Daniel's INT-31 answer): the report is rendered for PDF (`output: pdf`, TYP-71) with every chart drawn by the engine's vector renderer from its geometry model at its print width, so printing needs no WebGL. The conversion may take time; the export does not have to be instant (PRF-16). This card is the only definition of the pagination bar: no chart, figure, metric, callout or table row split (a table may break between rows and repeats its header); no heading last on a page; no page holding only the colophon or a source note; no bottom gap over a quarter page: when the next chart or figure does not fit in the space left, the text that follows it flows up to fill the page and the figure floats to the top of the next page, as LaTeX floats figures, so reading order may change around a figure (Daniel's choice, 2026-10-27); a gap over a quarter page is accepted only where the next block opens a new section and does not fit in the space left (Daniel, 2026-10-27, option 3 for the section-boundary cases). Floats keep their order, as in LaTeX: when several figures follow one another and the first does not fit, they float together, in order, and the text after them in the same section flows up to fill the page. Sections are float barriers: a figure never floats past the start of the next section, so when an unbreakable figure, or a run of figures, ends its section and does not fit, the page ends with that gap, as at any section boundary; every glyph in an embedded face; every chart drawn as vector paths and text, never as a raster image. items.title: Slides
items.question: Should a Rich Markdown source be able to render as slides, one screen per section, built for big numbers, charts and short text, shipped to users?
items.why: Daniel asked for it on 17 November 2026: internal reviews want screens of big bold numbers, charts, small text and headings, and the format should reach users too; on 19 November he asked for slides on the home page, no longer called experimental. It is a second rendition of the same source, so it reopens the “report HTML and its PDF are the only outputs” line of FEA-RP-46 and FEA-RP-47 without bringing the carousel or per-output markers back. INT-25 stands: RichView makes no slides from prompts; the author's agent writes them.
items.proposed:
**Slides are a second rendition of a Rich Markdown source.** `slides: true` in the frontmatter turns the source into slides. Each top-level heading or `---` starts a slide. The style's stage sets the look. The registry, `richview learn slides` and the guide open with these three lines. Slides were first built under an experimental label (17 November); Daniel dropped it on 19 November, so no render, check or page carries one.

**What the author writes.** An ordinary `.rmd` with `slides: true` in the frontmatter (TYP-100). Nothing else is new: the same prose, the same `metric`, `chart`, `table`, `callout` and `image` blocks, the same styles and the same checks. Removing the line gives the report back. No raw HTML, CSS or positions (INT-28).

**Where a slide starts.** The title, description, author and date make the title slide. Each top-level heading of the body (the ones a report's contents list) starts a slide and is its title. A thematic break (`---`) starts a slide without a title, for a screen that is only a number or a chart. Text before the first heading is a slide of its own.

**A big number is a `metric` block**, unchanged (FEA-RP-23): `value` with `unit`, `format` and `digits`; `label`; the change `delta` as a fraction; `delta_label` for what it is compared with (the period: `vs October`); `trend` when a fall is the good direction. One comparison per number, named in words, with its sign printed; colour only backs it up. On a slide the value is set in the display face at a size that follows the screen, and is fitted to its column by its character count, so a long value never leaves its box.

**Layout is automatic.** The author chooses what is on a slide, never where it sits. A slide has four regions in a fixed order: its title; a row of numbers; the figures; the text.

- Metrics stand in one row of equal columns, up to four; five to eight take two rows.
- A slide whose only content is one metric shows it as the hero: the largest number the format sets.
- Charts, tables and images are figures. One figure takes the room left; two stand side by side. A chart is laid out by the chart engine for the box it gets and at the screen's own resolution, with its lettering scaled to the stage; it is never a scaled picture. On a slide the numbers are the metrics: a chart prints none of the values it would add by itself (`auto_annotations` is `false` unless its author sets it), so no bar carries a number its neighbour lacks, and its actions (table, downloads, the expanded view) stay with the report the same source renders. Its bars take their category's share of the plot rather than the width a report's column caps them at, and two charts side by side share one card height. A table that is its slide's only figure keeps the slide's width, its text under it, and is set larger.
- Paragraphs, lists and callouts are the slide's text. Beside one figure it is a column a third of the slide wide; under two figures it runs the slide's width; alone it is set larger at the reading measure. A source note stays under its figure.
- A heading with nothing under it is a section slide.

**Density is checked, not hoped for.** A render and `richview check` warn `slides.density`, naming the slide and its line, when a slide holds more than four numbers beside a figure or more than eight in all, more than two figures, more than 50 words of text beside a figure or number (80 alone), or a table of more than ten rows. The fix is always the same: start a new slide. `slides.tabs` warns that `tabs` has no effect in slides. `collapsed_sections` (FEA-RP-67) has no effect either, without a warning: a slide shows everything it holds. Nor do columns (FEA-RP-68): their markers drop out before the cut, and what they hold takes its place in the slide's numbers, figures and text. A style's background (STY-74) stays behind the slides; a picture behind the header fills the title slide's stage, with the title on a solid panel, and on a phone it is the report's band above the title. These numbers are ours: the published ones are practitioner heuristics (3 to 4 big numbers, 2 to 3 views, a table past about eight cards), and no study stands behind 6×6 or 10/20/30.

**Fit.** On a landscape window of 900 px or more a slide is a 16:9 stage, as large as the window allows and centred. Every text size and gap is a share of the stage, so 1280 × 720, 1440 × 810 and 1920 × 1080 show the same composition: text at 2.7% of the stage's height and the smallest lettering at 2.1%, the sizes Apple sets for a television and the range AVIXA gives for a meeting room. On a narrower or portrait window (a phone) a slide is the window's width and at least its height: numbers stand two to a row, figures and text one under another, at the style's own sizes. Nothing is clipped and no text is shrunk to make it fit: a slide that needs more than one screen grows and scrolls.

**Each style has a stage.** A slides source stands on its style's stage, a world of its own built from the style's tokens and faces rather than one layout recoloured (STY-01). The style chooses it with the leaf `components.slides.stage` (TYP-48); the builtins set Sleek's `keynote`, Air's `gallery`, Brutalist's `poster`, Hand-drawn's `sketchbook` and Scientific's `paper`, and `plain` keeps the layout alone. A stage changes type, colour, framing and how a slide arrives, never what a slide holds or where it sits, and keeps its character on a phone at the style's own sizes.

- Keynote, a stage at night: the lone number and the section slides stand on a full field of the accent in white; the title is set large at the foot of its slide, its date a small line of capitals at the top; charts stand straight on the dark.
- Gallery, daylight on a Swiss grid: flush left; the lone number in the text face's light figures, in the accent, across the foot of the slide under its label; the section on the raised surface, the one quiet field.
- Poster, a wall of posters: condensed capitals to the edges between heavy bars; the lone number white on the accent's field over a heavy bar, the section on ink; numbers beside a figure as one band of knockout blocks; table heads on ink; each working slide's title under a short accent tag.
- Sketchbook, a talk drawn as it is given: lettering at a tilt, the title, the lone number and the section centred, the red pencil under each number.
- Paper, the talk of a good paper: a title page, headings over a rule, the lone number between two rules with its label in italic, figures and tables numbered as a paper numbers them ("Figure 2", "Table 1"), tables in booktabs rules.

On a field the counter and the progress bar take the field's ink, and up and down lose their colours: a change's sign and words carry it, as on STY-33's knockout. On a slide a chart stands on the stage rather than on a panel of its own; Poster keeps its outline.

**Every slide is a stage moment, not only the lone number and the section.** On a builtin style's stage the renderer marks only what the source tells it, and the stage sets each in its own manner:

- A slide about one chart, with no numbers, states the chart's title as its headline at display size; the slide's own title runs above it as its topic, at the text's size.
- In a row of two to four numbers the first leads, wider and larger, and the others support it: the first metric is taken as the slide's headline figure. Two to four numbers over one chart, with no text beside it, stand as a rail: a column on the left, the first leading, each as large as its share of the column's height allows, and the chart takes the slide's whole height beside them rather than the strip a row would leave it.
- A number's change is a chip that names its direction with a mark pointing up or down. Gallery and Paper set it as type, Poster boxes it in its ink, and Sketchbook rings the lone number's change in pencil.
- In a Markdown table a column whose every cell is a signed change (`+50%`, `−3.1 pp`) carries each as a chip; the number column just before a closing run of such columns, the latest one the changes compare, leads while the other number columns step back; and a last row whose every number column is the sum of the rows above it is ruled off as their total. What each cell says and the order of rows and columns stay as written.
- A slide of text sets its callout as a pull quote beside its points.
- A chart lets its first series lead in its colour while the others step back to quiet tones, keeps two to four gridlines and prints its values as in a report: on a stage the number is the message. A bar, line or area chart sets those values half again as large as its axes (about 1.8 stage units) and in the axis's compact form (`$420K`, not `$420 thousand`), as the slide's headlines write them, at the same precision (FEA-CH-37). On a light page a quiet tone keeps its own hue; on Keynote's night it is a slate of the page's own hue. Sketchbook's charts lead in its red pencil ahead of its greys. The lettering stays in the style's measured data face.
- The title slide is each stage's opening: Keynote's large type on the night stage with the accent's glow behind it, Gallery's huge light type over a foot of date and lede, Paper's title between the rules of its tables, its section slides between the same two rules, Sketchbook's lettered title over a red swash with its date ringed. Keynote's fields have depth, light from the upper left deepening to the foot, all from the field's own colour.

**Slides arrive.** A slide that starts below the first screen builds as it comes into view: its title, numbers, figures and text come in one after another at the pace of the style's motion (FEA-RP-35's tokens), each stage in its own manner: a rise (keynote and gallery, whose lone number rises from behind the slide's foot), a hard wipe (poster), a landing with a wobble and the red pencil drawn after it (sketchbook), a fade (paper). Nothing of a build stays once the slide has arrived. The first screen, a page without scripts, reduced motion, a style with motion off and paper show every slide at rest. Nothing waits for a key press: this is not a step-by-step reveal.

**Moving through them.** The slides are one vertical sequence that snaps to each slide, so the wheel, a trackpad and a swipe work as on any page. Space, Page Down, → and ↓ go on; Shift+Space, Page Up, ← and ↑ go back; Home and End go to the ends; `F` toggles full screen. Arrow keys and Space stay with a chart, table or control while it has focus. A counter (`4 / 12`) sits in a corner of the stage, and the report's progress bar fills as the slides pass. The address carries the slide (`#slide=4`, counted from 1) without adding history entries. Keys, counter and address live in the report runtime; no handwritten JavaScript is added (ARC-03). Without scripts the sequence, the snapping and the browser's own keys remain; the counter does not. Reduced motion jumps instead of gliding.

**Paper.** Printing from the browser gives one slide per page on a 16:9 landscape page (13.33 × 7.5 in), in the style's print colours, without the counter. `richview generate --to pdf` gives the same pages.

**Where it shows.** Slides are what the renderer returns for the source, so every surface that shows the rendered document in a window of its own shows slides: the exported file, `richview serve`, the hosted app (its bar stands above the first slide and scrolls away with it), the VS Code preview and the playground's preview pane. A page that frames a report at the height of its content cannot hold a screen-high slide: a Publish story is one. A publication shows a slides source as the report.

**Not in this card:** speaker notes, step-by-step reveals, transitions between slides, per-slide layout keywords, backgrounds or images an author sets behind a slide, an overview grid, a measured overflow check, PowerPoint or Google Slides export, and new `metric` fields (a sparkline, a target, an absolute change). Each returns as its own card.
